title: Threads from zero
goal: By the end you can say what a thread is and what it costs, start threads with `start()` and wait for them with `join()`, and split a job across several workers.
opening:
Picture the nightly settlement job. It totals a day of card payments, a million of them, one after another on a single thread. The pod has four cores, and three of them sit idle while it runs. Your lead asks the obvious question: "Can't we split it across four threads?"

It sounds like a ten-minute change. Yet the first version people write usually compiles, passes every test and runs no faster than before. That isn't carelessness. A `Thread` looks like any other Java object with a few ordinary methods, and the method that sounds as if it runs the thread doesn't.

You already work with threads every day, even if you've never created one. Every Quarkus request and every Kafka record you handle runs on a thread that someone else started. In this lesson, we'll meet the threads a JVM already has, split the settlement total across threads of our own, and measure what that buys us. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: `main` starts a thread that prints "done" after 2 seconds. Then `main` returns at once. What happens?
options: The program exits at once and "done" never prints
"done" prints after about 2 seconds, then the program exits
An IllegalThreadStateException is thrown because main ended first
It depends on how many cores the machine has
warmup.why: The JVM keeps running until every non-daemon thread has finished, and the threads you create are non-daemon unless you say otherwise. Returning from `main` ends the main thread and nothing else. So the worker carries on, prints "done", and only then does the JVM exit. The core count changes how fast things run, not whether the JVM waits. We'll watch it happen in the last section.

sections.body:
Let's begin with the emptiest program we can write: a `main` method that only asks the JVM which threads exist. Before our code has started a single thread, the list already has six:

```text
Reference Handler (daemon)
Finalizer (daemon)
Common-Cleaner (daemon)
Signal Dispatcher (daemon)
main
Notification Thread (daemon)
```

That list comes from the first Try it below, run on JDK 21. `main` runs your code. The others are helpers the JVM starts for itself. The garbage collector and the JIT compiler have threads of their own as well, and those don't even show up in this list. (The JIT compiler is the part of the JVM that turns hot bytecode into machine code while your program runs.) So you've been writing multithreaded programs all along.

Two words will carry us through this track. A **process** is a running program with its own memory. Your payment service in its container is one process, and no other process can read its memory. A **thread** is one path of execution inside a process. It runs one statement after another, and always knows where it is in the code.

The threads of one process split their memory in a simple way. Picture a restaurant kitchen. The cooks share one fridge and one set of counters, but each cook works from their own order ticket on their own cutting board. In programming terms, each cook is a thread. The fridge and counters are the **heap**: every object you create with `new` and every `static` field lives there, and any thread with a reference can reach it. The ticket and board are the thread's **stack**: its local variables, its parameters and the chain of calls in progress. No other thread can see them.

That split explains most of this track. Sharing the heap is what makes threads useful: one thread puts a `Payment` into a map and another reads it, with no copying and no network. It's also what makes them dangerous, because two threads can change the same object at the same moment. Lesson 3 of this track (Race conditions: why count++ lies) shows how that quietly loses money.

You may be thinking, "I never create threads. Quarkus does that for me." That only means someone else created them. Take a thread dump of one of your services with `jcmd <pid> Thread.print` and count. You'll find event-loop threads, worker threads for blocking code, Kafka client threads, connection-pool housekeepers and the JVM's own helpers. On a pod with two cores, that's often well over a hundred. Your request handler runs on one of them. Whatever it puts on the heap, the others can reach.

**Locals belong to one thread. The heap belongs to all of them.** So when you ask whether some code is thread-safe, start with one question: which of its values live on the heap?

Six threads, and we haven't started one yet. Let's start some of our own and put those idle cores to work.

try.title: Meet the threads you already have
steps: Run `HelloThreads` with the command below. It lists the threads that exist before `main` starts any, then starts two of its own.
Look at the list. Which of these threads are daemons? (A daemon thread is one the JVM doesn't wait for when it exits. The last section of this lesson comes back to that.)
Now run it three more times and watch the two `hello` lines. Does `worker-a` always speak first?

code.title: HelloThreads.java

alt.title: HelloThreads.kt

try.expect: You'll see `main` and five daemon helpers, in an order that can change from run to run. The two workers usually print in the order they were started, but not always: in one run on a 4-core Linux machine, `worker-b` said hello first. Nothing in the code promises an order, so the scheduler is free to pick. Code that depends on that order is a bug waiting for a busy day.

sections.h: Splitting the total across four threads

aside.title: Why not just call parallelStream()?
aside.body: You could. For a plain sum, `amounts.parallelStream().mapToLong(Long::longValue).sum()` does the whole job in one line (in Kotlin, `amounts.parallelStream().mapToLong { it }.sum()`). Underneath, it does what we're doing by hand: it splits the list, sums the pieces on threads, and combines the results. Those threads come from the JVM-wide common `ForkJoinPool`, which by default has one thread fewer than you have cores, because the calling thread joins in. We build the split by hand once, so that you know what that one line costs and where it can go wrong. The lesson ForkJoinPool, work stealing and parallel streams, in the executors track, picks it up from there.

try.title: Break it with run()
steps: In `HelloThreads`, change `a.start()` and `b.start()` to `a.run()` and `b.run()`. Before you run it, predict the two "hello from" lines.
Run it with the same command as the first Try it.
Now put the `start()` calls back, and add a second `a.start();` right after the first one. What do you expect this time? Run it and see.
try.expect: With `run()`, both lines say `hello from main`. No new thread was ever created, and the two joins return at once, because a thread that never started has nothing to wait for. With the double `start()`, `main` dies with an `IllegalThreadStateException`, yet `worker-a` still prints its line, because the first `start()` worked. A thread runs once, and only `start()` runs it.

sections.h: Measuring the speedup, and where it stops
sections.body:
Look back at the first line `HelloThreads` printed. Here it said `cores the JVM sees: 4`, and that number decides how much our four workers can buy.

A CPU core runs one thread at a time. (Hyper-threading lets one physical core run two, each a little slower.) `Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors()` tells you how many the JVM may use. Inside a container it follows the CPU limit, so a pod with `cpu: 2` reports 2.

Your service has far more threads than cores, and the operating system's scheduler makes that work. It lets a thread run for a short slice of time, then saves its registers and switches to another thread. (Registers are the handful of values a core is working on.) That's a **context switch**. It happens thousands of times a second, which is why 200 threads on 4 cores all seem to make progress. Back in the kitchen, the stoves are the cores. With more cooks than stoves, the cooks take turns. That's fine while most of them are waiting for water to boil, and pointless when every one of them needs a stove.

Two words get mixed up here, so let's pin them down:

- **Concurrency** is about structure: several tasks are in progress at the same time. It works on one core, by taking turns.
- **Parallelism** is about hardware: several tasks run at the same instant, on different cores.

Our four settlement workers are concurrent on any machine. They run fully in parallel only when four cores are free for them.

So here's my guess before we time anything. Two threads should take about half the time of one, four threads about a quarter, and eight threads should be no better than four.

Now the measurement. Summing a million longs takes a few milliseconds, too quick to time honestly, and a real settlement job does far more work per payment anyway. So the `ParallelSum` demo below stands in for that work with 400 million small sums of pure arithmetic, split over 1, 2, 4 and 8 threads. It runs a few warm-up rounds first, so that the JIT has compiled the loop before we time it. On a 4-core Linux machine, one run printed 510 ms, 257 ms, 121 ms and 125 ms.

Correctness first: every run printed the same checksum, so splitting the work lost nothing. Then speed. Two threads halved the time, and four threads cut it to about a quarter, as we guessed. (Slightly better than four times, which is just the noise of one short run.) Eight threads were no faster than four. The extra four threads had no cores of their own, so they took turns on the same four.

That wall is for work that keeps a core busy. Waiting work is different. A thread waiting 120 ms for the card issuer uses no core while it waits. So a service that mostly waits can usefully run many more threads than it has cores.

**CPU-bound work wants one thread per core. Waiting work can use many more.** The executors track turns that into a sizing formula.

So threads can buy real speed, up to the core count. They aren't free, though, and they have one more habit that surprises people at shutdown. Let's look at both.

try.title: Find the core count by timing
steps: Check how many cores your machine has. Then write down a guess for 1, 2, 4 and 8 threads.
Run `ParallelSum` with the command below. Every run does the same 400 million additions, split across the threads.
Compare the times with your guess. Where does adding threads stop helping?

code.title: ParallelSum.java

alt.title: ParallelSum.kt

try.expect: The bend in the curve sits at your core count. Each doubling roughly halves the time until the threads outnumber the cores, and after that the extra threads just take turns. If your machine is busy with something else, the curve flattens. On a 4-core machine with other heavy builds running, one run printed 498, 422, 410 and 326 ms. Our threads were now sharing the cores with other programs, and eight threads even came out ahead, because the scheduler shares the cores out thread by thread, so more threads got more turns. Measure on a quiet machine, and run it more than once.

sections.h: What a thread costs, and who the JVM waits for
sections.body:
Every `Thread` we've created so far is a **platform thread**: one Java thread backed by one operating system thread. That has a price, in memory and in time.

Memory first. Each platform thread gets its own stack, and on 64-bit Linux the JVM reserves 1 MB for it by default. (`java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version` shows `ThreadStackSize = 1024`, in KB.) The operating system commits that memory only as the stack grows, so a thread with shallow calls uses much less. Still, 10,000 threads means 10 GB of reserved address space and 10,000 kernel threads sharing the cores. Somewhere along that road, your service dies with an `OutOfMemoryError` that says it is unable to create a native thread.

Then time. Creating, starting and ending a thread is a round trip to the kernel. The `ThreadCost` demo starts and joins 10,000 empty threads, and on a 4-core Linux machine it printed about 130 microseconds per thread. For one 120 ms call to the card issuer, that's noise. For a new thread per Kafka record at 5,000 records a second, it's most of a core spent on starting and ending threads. That cost is why the executors track reuses threads in pools, and why the virtual threads track exists at all.

Now back to the warm-up question. The JVM exits when the last **non-daemon** thread ends, or when something calls `System.exit`. Returning from `main` ends the main thread and nothing else, so a worker that's still settling a batch keeps the JVM alive until it's done. Threads are non-daemon unless you say otherwise.

**Returning from `main` ends one thread, not the program.**

That's the whole toolkit of this lesson, so let's be honest about where it stops. A new thread per task suits four long slices. For thousands of short tasks, starting the threads can cost more than the work itself. A worker that fails dies alone: if its `run()` throws, the thread ends, its stack trace goes to standard error, and `main` isn't told, because `join()` simply returns. And while we can wait for a thread to finish, we have no way yet to ask a running thread to stop.

try.title: Measure a thread, then let main go first
steps: Run `ThreadCost` with `./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l01.ThreadCost`. It starts and joins 10,000 empty threads, three rounds in a row. Note the microseconds per thread.
Now read `MainEndsFirst` below. `main` starts one worker and returns at once. How many "settling batch" lines will print? Commit to a number.

code.title: MainEndsFirst.java

alt.title: MainEndsFirst.kt

try.expect: `ThreadCost` prints tens to a couple of hundred microseconds per thread on most machines. Under heavy load it can be far more: with other builds running alongside, a 4-core Linux machine printed 900 to 1,300. `MainEndsFirst` prints `main: returning from main()` first, then all five batches and `worker: all batches settled`. The JVM waited for the non-daemon worker, long after `main` was gone.

compare.title: Starting and joining workers in Java and Kotlin

java.title: Java

kotlin.title: KotlinThreads.kt

compare.note: Kotlin's `thread { }` is a small standard-library function. It builds a `java.lang.Thread`, sets its options and calls `start()` for you, unless you pass `start = false`, so forgetting `start()` mostly stops being a mistake you can make. Kotlin has no checked exceptions, so `join()` needs no `throws InterruptedException`. The interruption rules still apply, and lesson 2 of this track covers them. One more difference shows in the loop. A Java lambda can only capture effectively final locals, which is why the Java code copies `w` into `slot`. The Kotlin lambda captures the `w` parameter of `List(4) { w -> }` directly.

worked.title: Split a settlement total across four threads

steps.say: Let's write the fixed version properly, the way the lab wants it. We have one million settled amounts in a `List<Long>` and four workers. First, the slices: each worker gets a contiguous range, and the remainder is spread out so that sizes differ by at most one.
steps.alt_code:
val slices = minOf(workers, amounts.size)   // no idle threads
val base = amounts.size / slices
val extra = amounts.size % slices             // the first `extra` slices get one more

steps.say: Next, one slot per worker. Worker 2 writes only `partial[2]`, so no two threads ever write the same memory, and there's nothing for them to race on.
steps.code:
long[] partial = new long[slices];
Thread[] threads = new Thread[slices];
steps.alt_code:
val partial = LongArray(slices)
val threads = ArrayList<Thread>(slices)

steps.say: Now start every thread. Before you read on, ask yourself: what would happen if you called `join()` inside this same loop, right after `start()`?

Joining inside the loop would wait for worker 0 before starting worker 1, and we'd be back to one thread at a time. So start them all, then join them all. Only after the last join is it safe to read `partial`, because `join()` makes each worker's write visible to the caller.

lab.title: Total a day of payments on N threads
steps: Run the tests once. All six fail with `UnsupportedOperationException`.
Work out the slices: `Math.min(workers, size)` threads, contiguous ranges, sizes that differ by at most one.
Start one named thread per slice. Each thread sums its slice into its own slot of a `long[]`.
Join every thread, then add up the slots and return the total. Run the tests until all six pass.
hints: One test wraps the list so it can record which threads call `get`. It fails if the caller reads any amount itself, or if the number of reading threads isn't the number of slices.
A lambda can only use local variables that never change. Copy loop variables into fresh locals (`int slot = w;`) before the lambda.
If the totals come out wrong only sometimes, check that you read `partial` after the joins, not before. That's the impatient total from the second section.

drill.title: Start, then join, from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write a `main` that starts three threads named `fx-0`, `fx-1` and `fx-2`. Each one prints its own name. `main` waits for all three, then prints `all done`. When you compare with the answer, check one thing first: did you start all three before joining any?

alt.title: Kotlin

recap: A process has its own memory. Its threads share the heap (objects, static fields), and each thread has a private stack (locals, calls in progress).
`start()` creates a thread, which then calls `run()`. Call `run()` yourself and the code runs on the current thread, with no warning.
`join()` waits for a thread to end and makes its writes visible to you. Start every worker, then join them all, then read the results.
Concurrency is many tasks in progress; parallelism is many running at the same instant. CPU-bound work stops getting faster at about one thread per core, while a waiting thread uses no core.
The JVM exits when the last non-daemon thread ends. Returning from `main` ends only the main thread.

The limit: a platform thread is an OS thread, with 1 MB of stack reserved by default on 64-bit Linux and a trip to the kernel to create. A new thread per small task doesn't scale, and a worker that fails dies without telling anyone.
closing:
We started with a settlement job on one thread and three idle cores. We found six threads before our first line of code. We made the `run()` mistake and the impatient-total mistake, fixed both with `start()` and `join()`, and watched the speedup stop at the core count.

Now open one of your own services and search for `new Thread(` (and `thread {` in Kotlin). For each hit, ask who waits for that thread, and how. If the answer is a `Thread.sleep`, or nobody, you've found an impatient total.

Next, we'll follow one thread through its whole life, and answer the question this lesson left open: how do you stop a thread that doesn't want to finish?

options: audit
main
Thread-0
Nothing, because the thread was never started
quiz.why: `run()` is an ordinary method call, so the lambda runs on the thread that called it, and that's `main`. No new thread ever exists. You'd see `audit` only with `t.start()`. It does print something, though: `run()` executes the code, just on the wrong thread.

quiz.q: A batch job scores transactions with a fraud model. It is pure CPU work, with no I/O. The pod has 4 cores. Which thread count gives about the best throughput?
quiz.why: Pure CPU work keeps a core busy, and each core runs one thread at a time. Four threads keep all four cores working. More threads only take turns on the same cores and add context switches, just as the 8-thread run of `ParallelSum` showed. Counts like 400 make sense only when most threads spend their time waiting.

quiz.q: A worker thread throws a `NullPointerException` out of its `run()` method. What happens to `main`, which started it?
options: `main` gets the NullPointerException at its next line
The JVM shuts down
`main` carries on. The worker ends and its stack trace is printed to standard error
`main` gets it when it calls `join()`
quiz.why: An uncaught exception ends only the thread that threw it. The default handler prints the stack trace to standard error, and nobody else is told: `join()` simply returns once the worker has ended. Getting the exception back to the caller is a job for `Future`, in the executors track.

options: Nothing. It runs the jobs in parallel
It runs the jobs one at a time, because each join waits before the next thread starts
It deadlocks on the second job
`join()` must be called before `start()`
quiz.why: Each `join()` blocks until that thread ends, so the next thread starts only after the previous one has finished. You pay for a thread per job and still get one job at a time. Start every thread in one loop, then join them in a second loop.

quiz.q: A Kafka consumer service handles 12 partitions with 12 threads on a 2-core pod. Each record waits about 50 ms on Oracle. Which statement is true?
options: It is concurrent: 12 records are in progress, at most 2 threads run at any instant, and most are waiting anyway
It is parallel: all 12 threads run at the same instant
It cannot work, because threads must not outnumber cores
It is neither concurrent nor parallel
quiz.why: Twelve records in progress at once is concurrency. With 2 cores, at most 2 threads run at the same instant, and that's the parallel part. Each thread spends most of its time waiting on the database and uses no core while it waits, so 12 threads on 2 cores is a sensible setup. One thread per core is the rule for CPU-bound work.

flashcards.front: What do threads in one process share, and what does each thread have of its own?
flashcards.back: They share the heap: objects and static fields. Each thread has its own stack: local variables, parameters and the calls in progress.

flashcards.front: What happens if you call `t.run()` instead of `t.start()`?
flashcards.back: The code runs on the current thread, like any method call. No new thread is created, and nothing warns you.

flashcards.front: Concurrency vs parallelism, in one line each.
flashcards.back: Concurrency: several tasks in progress at the same time (works on one core). Parallelism: several tasks running at the same instant on different cores.
When the last non-daemon thread ends, or when something calls `System.exit`. Returning from `main` ends only the main thread.

flashcards.front: How much stack does the JVM reserve for a platform thread on 64-bit Linux by default?
flashcards.back: 1 MB (`ThreadStackSize = 1024` KB). It is reserved address space, committed as the stack grows. Change it with `-Xss`.

flashcards.front: What happens when you call `start()` twice on the same Thread?
flashcards.back: The second call throws `IllegalThreadStateException`. A thread runs at most once.

flashcards.front: A worker thread throws an uncaught exception. Who finds out?
flashcards.back: Only that thread dies. The default handler prints the stack trace to standard error. The starting thread is not told.

terms.plain: A running program with its own memory, such as one JVM.
One path of execution inside a process, with its own stack, sharing the process heap.
The memory where objects and static fields live. Every thread can reach it.
A piece of the CPU that runs one thread at a time.
The OS pausing one thread and resuming another on the same core.
Several tasks in progress at once, taking turns or not.
Several tasks running at the same instant on different cores.
A Java thread backed one-to-one by an operating system thread.

explain_back.prompt: A colleague moved a slow report onto "four threads" by writing `new Thread(job).run()` four times. All the tests pass, but the report is exactly as slow as before. Explain to them, in your own words, what happened and how to fix it.
explain_back.answer: `run()` is just a method call, so each job ran on the calling thread, one after the other. No new thread was ever created, which is why nothing got faster and nothing failed. `start()` is the call that creates a thread and has it call `run()`. So call `start()` on all four threads first, then `join()` each one before reading the results. That way the jobs really overlap, and `join()` makes their results visible to the caller.

deeper.body:
Since JDK 21 there's a builder API for threads. It's worth knowing now, because the virtual threads track uses the same shape:

```java
Thread t = Thread.ofPlatform()
        .name("ledger-worker-", 0)   // ledger-worker-0, ledger-worker-1, ...
        .start(task);
```

```kotlin
val t = Thread.ofPlatform()
    .name("ledger-worker-", 0)       // ledger-worker-0, ledger-worker-1, ...
    .start(task)
```

`Thread.ofPlatform()` gives you the same kind of thread as `new Thread(...)`. `Thread.ofVirtual()` gives you a virtual thread, which isn't tied to one OS thread and costs far less. That's a whole track of its own.

If you're curious about the threads the JVM keeps for itself, run `jcmd <pid> Thread.print` against any running Java process. Besides the Java threads from the first Try it, you'll see entries such as `VM Thread`, the JIT compiler threads and the garbage collector's workers. They live inside the JVM itself, so `Thread.getAllStackTraces()` doesn't list them, but they use cores and memory like any other thread.

One more cost to keep in mind: a context switch isn't free. The kernel saves and restores registers, and the incoming thread often finds the CPU caches full of the previous thread's data. That's part of why `ParallelSum` stops improving past the core count, and why a thousand busy threads can run slower than ten.
